en: The Country Doctor Who Worked Out How Glaciers Move
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / 🧊 Sveinn Pálsson

en: In **1793** a country doctor stood in front of one of these tongues and worked out something nobody in Europe had: **glaciers flow.** They are not frozen still. **They move like extremely slow treacle** — and he was right about a hundred years early.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / 🧊 Sveinn Pálsson

en: **Sveinn Pálsson**, **1762–1840**, was Iceland's first university-trained doctor and covered a district you would now call impossible — on horseback, alone, in this weather.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / 🧊 Sveinn Pálsson

en: He climbed and described these glaciers on his own time. His conclusion was that the ice **behaves like a viscous fluid**, deforming under its own weight and creeping downhill. That is the modern answer.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / 🧊 Sveinn Pálsson

en: Europe was not ready for it. **His glacier work was not properly published until the twentieth century**, long after he died — so the credit for glacier flow went elsewhere and he spent his life as the local doctor.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / 🧊 Sveinn Pálsson

en: He also had the day job. A district physician here in the eighteenth century meant riding to a farm across a glacial river in the dark, with whatever was in the bag.

en: The Benedictine house was founded in **1186** and ran until the **Reformation in 1550.** Tradition, via *Landnámabók*, says the **Papar** — Irish monks — were here before the Norse, and that the ground was so blessed no heathen could settle on it.

en: The place-names still gossip about the nuns: **Systrafoss**, the sisters' falls; the lake **Systravatn**; and **Systrastapi**, the rock where the darker version has two sisters burned for sin and cleared only afterwards.

en: **Kirkjugólf** — the 'church floor' — is a patch of **columnar basalt** worn flat until it looks tiled. Nobody laid it. **The volcano did the tiling**, and the glacier and the sea planed it level.

en: And this is where **Rev. Jón Steingrímsson** preached the **Eldmessa, the Fire Sermon, on 20 July 1783**, with the Laki lava coming down the valley. It stopped at the edge of the parish. He kept preaching.

en: The Biggest Lava Flood in Recorded History
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / 🌋 Eldgjá

en: Everyone knows Laki. **Eldgjá was bigger** — and it is the most powerful eruption Iceland has produced in ten thousand years.
ctx: opening hook line — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / 🌋 Eldgjá

en: It began in the **spring of 939** and ran on, at least in episodes, **into the autumn of 940**, along a fissure **75 kilometres** long. The flow travelled **about 70 kilometres** to the sea.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / 🌋 Eldgjá

en: Volume: **about 20 km³** of lava, against Laki's **14.7.** Vísindavefur rates it **VEI-6** and puts it **a full magnitude and a half above Laki** on the magnitude scale — which is why it calls Eldgjá **the most powerful Icelandic eruption of the last ten thousand years.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / 🌋 Eldgjá

en: **VEI-6 is rare company.** Across ten thousand years only a handful of Icelandic eruptions reach it — the **Saksunarvatn** event, **Veiðivötn in 1477**, and this one. Eldgjá came **about 840 years before Lakagígar.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / 🌋 Eldgjá

en: And here is the part that lands: it happened **in living memory of the settlement.** People were here. They watched it.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Fellsfjara → Vík 2 hour drive folks / 🌋 Eldgjá

en: The whole belt between **Mýrdalsjökull** and **Vatnajökull** is made of these — **Lakagígar, Eldgjá, Veiðivötn, Vatnaöldur.** Four names, four gashes, one neighbourhood. Vísindavefur states plainly that **another great fissure eruption in this belt is all but certain** — Grímsvötn, Katla or Bárðarbunga — and that it could come very soon or in many centuries.

en: The Man Who Refused to Settle
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🦈 Bjarnarhöfn

en: The man who took that land was called **Björn the Easterner** — and he got the name because he **refused to settle in the west.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🦈 Bjarnarhöfn

en: *Landnámabók* is blunt about it. Björn, son of **Ketill flatnefur**, was driven off the family's Norwegian estates by **King Haraldur hárfagri**, went west over the sea, *"og vildi þar ekki staðfestast"* — **and would not settle there.** So they named him for the direction he wouldn't stop facing.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🦈 Bjarnarhöfn

en: He took the land between **Hraunsfjörður** and **Stafá**, kept a magnificent household — and **died unbaptised**, the only one of Ketill's children who never took the faith. No churchyard: a heathen mound by **Borgarlækur**. When an archaeologist went looking for it in **1900**, he found the stream had eaten both the mound and the farm. Nothing left to look at.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🦈 Bjarnarhöfn

en: The genealogy is the gift: Björn → Óttar → Helgi → **Ósvífur hinn spaki** → **Guðrún Ósvífursdóttir**. **The most famous woman in the Icelandic sagas is his great-great-granddaughter.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🦈 Bjarnarhöfn

en: **The church is 1856–58** and is **the last of its kind standing.** One builder from Grundarfjörður put up three towered churches on this peninsula in the 1850s — Helgafell, Skarð and this one. **The other two are gone.** This one lost its tower around 1900 and survived precisely because nobody thought it worth replacing. Seven metres by four and a half, inside.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🦈 Bjarnarhöfn

en: And the shark. **Everything you have heard about how it is made is wrong.** The Greenland shark **has no urinary system**, so urea builds up in the flesh and breaks down to **ammonia** — that is the toxin. **Nobody urinates on it.** Vísindavefur calls that idea *"mikill misskilningur."* At Bjarnarhöfn it ferments **six to eight weeks in slatted wooden boxes**, then hangs **six to eight weeks more** in the drying shed. Not buried in gravel, not any more.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🦈 Bjarnarhöfn

en: In **2023 Matís** — the national food research institute — noted that **almost no scientific work had ever been done on how Icelanders make their national dish.** A thousand years of it, and the first proper study was a master's thesis, done with this farm.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🦈 Bjarnarhöfn

en: The Mountain You Walk Into When You Die
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / ⛰️ Helgafell

en: There is a mountain out there that people believed they went **into** when they died — and one autumn evening a shepherd stood on the hill and watched **the north side open up.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / ⛰️ Helgafell

en: **Þórólfur Mostrarskegg** held it so sacred that **no one was to look at it unwashed**, and nothing on it — beast or man — was to be harmed. *"Það var trúa þeirra Þórólfs frænda, að þeir dæi allir í fjallið"* — **he and his kin believed they would all die into the mountain.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / ⛰️ Helgafell

en: *Eyrbyggja saga*, chapter 11: a shepherd north of Helgafell **saw the mountain open**, saw great fires inside, and **heard Þorsteinn þorskabítur being welcomed in and told to sit in the high seat facing his father.** Next morning men rode in from Höskuldsey with the news. **Þorsteinn had drowned that day.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / ⛰️ Helgafell

en: **Snorri goði** — remember him — farmed there **thirty-one years**, and when he had a problem he walked up it: *"Þau ráð hafa síst að engu orðið er þar hafa ráðin verið"* — **"the plans laid up there have least often come to nothing."** It is where he and Víga-Styrr sat the day they decided what to do about the berserkers.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / ⛰️ Helgafell

en: He is also **the man who ended the argument at the conversion.** When a messenger reported lava flowing and the heathens cried that the gods were angry, Snorri asked: *"Um hvað reiddust goðin þá, er hér brann hraunið, er nú stöndum vér á?"* — **"What were the gods angry about, then, when the lava we are standing on was burning?"** That is *Kristni saga*, and it is the same man from this hillside.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / ⛰️ Helgafell

en: **Be careful with the three wishes.** Walk in silence from Guðrún's grave, don't look back, don't tell anyone — every guidebook prints it. **The earliest written record of it is 1955.** The Icelandic living-heritage register says so plainly. It is real folklore and it is **younger than rock and roll.** It appears nowhere in Eyrbyggja or Laxdæla.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / ⛰️ Helgafell

en: And the grave itself: the State's own protection register calls it **"leiði Guðrúnar Ósvífursdóttur, svo nefnt"** — **the *so-called* grave.** The one man who dug there, **W. G. Collingwood in 1897**, never gave the lecture he promised and never handed the finds in. **Nobody actually knows where she lies.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / ⛰️ Helgafell

en: Fifty Thousand Tonnes of Herring
ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🌊 Kolgrafarfjörður

en: On the water we are crossing right now, **about fifty thousand tonnes of herring suffocated** across two winters. **There is no comparable event recorded anywhere on Earth.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🌊 Kolgrafarfjörður

en: The fjord was crossed in **2004** — an embankment and a bridge with a water opening of about **150 metres**, shortening the road to Stykkishólmur by six kilometres. Inside it the fjord is about **10 km²** and up to **40 m** deep.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🌊 Kolgrafarfjörður

en: The herring came back after a long absence. They **began wintering in southern Breiðafjörður in 2006**, having been gone since roughly **1940**. By **2008** Hafrannsóknastofnun measured **800,000 to 900,000 tonnes** in the bay. **The day before it happened, close to 300,000 tonnes of live herring were sitting in this one fjord.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🌊 Kolgrafarfjörður

en: **13–14 December 2012: around 25–30,000 tonnes died.** Then **1 February 2013: another 22,000.** Cause — **oxygen depletion**. Prolonged calm, cold weather, and simply too much fish in too small a space. And once December's dead began to rot, **the decomposition ate the remaining oxygen**, which is why it happened again six weeks later.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🌊 Kolgrafarfjörður

en: **Now the correction, because everyone blames the bridge.** Verkfræðistofan Vatnaskil reported for Vegagerðin on **21 October 2015**: **the causeway was not the cause.** It may marginally worsen oxygen levels during a huge influx in bad conditions, but the effect is **negligible** against what the herring themselves did — and **worse conditions have occurred since with no die-off.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Selvallafoss → Kirkjufell / 🌊 Kolgrafarfjörður

en: This headland is where geologists proved the Ice Age **wasn't one long winter.** The evidence is seashells — sitting **high above the sea.**
ctx: opening hook line — tour 9.0 / Kirkjufell → Ólafsvík / 🐚 Búlandshöfði

en: High in this cliff are **marine fossil beds** — shells, laid down on a seabed — now stranded far above the present shore, and **sealed under lava dated to roughly 1.1 million years.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Kirkjufell → Ólafsvík / 🐚 Búlandshöfði

en: That is the whole argument. Shells mean **open, ice-free sea.** Lava on top means an eruption came afterwards. Stack the layers and you are reading **warm interglacials sandwiched between cold stages** — the Ice Age switching on and off, written into a cliff face.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Kirkjufell → Ólafsvík / 🐚 Búlandshöfði

en: It made Búlandshöfði **a classic site in Icelandic Quaternary geology.** Generations of students have been driven out here to look at the rock above your window.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Kirkjufell → Ólafsvík / 🐚 Búlandshöfði

en: Honest caveat: **you cannot pick the shell beds out from the road.** They are high in the face and you need someone standing next to you pointing. Point at the cliff, not at a layer.

en: **Geirríður** of **Mávahlíð** was accused of being a **kveldriða** — a night-rider — of riding a man in his sleep until he sickened and died. In most of medieval Europe that accusation had one ending.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Kirkjufell → Ólafsvík / 🧙 Mávahlíð

en: Not here. The charge was brought to the **þing**, argued, and **Geirríður was acquitted** — the accuser could not make it stand. *Eyrbyggja saga* records the whole thing as a legal matter, because that is what it was.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Kirkjufell → Ólafsvík / 🧙 Mávahlíð

en: Keep the chronology straight, because guests always ask about burnings. Iceland's actual witch-hunt was the **17th century** — the first burning for witchcraft was **1625**, the last **1685.** Of roughly **25 Icelanders** ever burned, the overwhelming majority were **men.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Kirkjufell → Ólafsvík / 🧙 Mávahlíð

en: So the picture people arrive with — medieval Iceland burning women — is the wrong century **and** the wrong gender. Here, in the saga age, the answer to a witchcraft accusation was a hearing.
